analogy.p: Background radiation is like the quiet background noise in a classroom: it is always there, from lots of small sources such as the corridor, the ventilation and the road. If you want to measure how loud one student is speaking, you must first measure the background noise on its own, then subtract it from the total to find the student's contribution. This is exactly how corrected count rate works. Where it breaks down: background noise is easy to hear but radiation is invisible, and the level of background noise can be reduced by closing a door whereas background radiation cannot be switched off.

bullets: Know the **sources of background radiation**: natural (radon, cosmic rays, rocks, food) and man-made (fallout from weapons tests, nuclear accidents, medical).
Know that the **level of background radiation varies** with location and with occupation.
Know that radiation **dose** is measured in **sieverts (Sv)**; **1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv)**.
Know that radiation can **damage living cells**, causing mutation, cancer or cell death.
Know **uses in medicine**: tracers, radiotherapy and sterilising equipment, plus other uses such as smoke detectors and thickness gauges.
Be able to **evaluate** risks and benefits and explain why a source is suited to a use.
Know why research into radiation effects is **published and peer reviewed**.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This spec point covers three linked ideas. First, **background radiation**: its natural and man-made sources, how it varies with location and occupation, and how it is measured. Second, the **hazards** of ionising radiation, including how **radiation dose** is measured in **sieverts (Sv)**. Third, the **uses of nuclear radiation**, especially in **medicine** (exploration of internal organs and control or destruction of unwanted tissue), and how to **evaluate the perceived risks** against the benefits. Examiners want you to match the type of radiation and half-life to the job, and to justify the choice.

bullets: It is **always present**, so a Geiger-Muller tube with no source nearby still gives a small count rate.
It is made of alpha, beta and gamma radiation from many sources.
On average, **natural sources contribute most** of the dose people receive.
Background radiation is **very low level**, and the body is used to it.
The size of background radiation **changes from place to place and over time**.
Measuring background is essential for finding the real count rate from a source (see later).
It is not caused by the experiment, so it is subtracted from readings.
It is the reason your count rate is never exactly zero.
core.p: **Background radiation** is the low-level ionising radiation that is **around us all the time**. It is present everywhere on Earth, even when there is no obvious radioactive source nearby, so any measurement of a radioactive source must take it into account. It comes from both **natural sources** and **man-made sources**. Most of it is natural and has always existed; human activity adds a smaller amount on average.

bullets: **Radon gas**: radioactive gas released from rocks (e.g. granite); it is an **alpha emitter**, so it is most dangerous when **inhaled**.
**Cosmic rays**: high-energy particles from the Sun and space; the dose is greater at high altitude.
**Rocks and buildings**: contain traces of uranium, thorium and other radioactive isotopes.
**Food and drink**: plants and animals take in small amounts of radioactive isotopes, e.g. potassium-40.
The human body itself contains small amounts of radioactive isotopes.
The atmosphere absorbs much cosmic radiation, so levels rise with altitude.
Areas with granite rocks (for example parts of Cornwall and Aberdeen) tend to have more radon.
Radon dangers can be reduced by improved ventilation and sealed floors.
core.p: Natural background radiation comes from the Earth, from space and from living things. The biggest single natural source is **radon gas**, produced by the decay of uranium in rocks such as granite. Radon seeps out of the ground and can collect inside buildings, where people may breathe it in. Other natural sources include **cosmic rays** from space and the Sun, the **rocks and soil** we live on and the **building materials** made from them, and **food and drink**, which contain small amounts of radioactive isotopes such as potassium-40.

bullets: **Fallout from nuclear weapons testing**: radioactive dust spread through the atmosphere and then fell to the ground.
**Nuclear accidents** (for example Chernobyl) released radioactive material into the environment.
**Medical sources**: X-rays, CT scans and nuclear medicine procedures contribute to dose.
**Nuclear power and waste**: normal operation adds only a very small amount to the average dose.
Man-made sources are generally a **smaller share** of the average background than natural sources.
Individual doses from man-made sources vary greatly, for example a person who has had many scans.
The risk from medical radiation is small and is outweighed by the benefit of diagnosis.
Man-made contamination can persist where long half-life isotopes were released.
core.p: Man-made sources are produced by human activities. Examples named in the specification include **fallout from nuclear weapons tests** and **nuclear accidents**. Radioactive material from these events was spread through the atmosphere and settled on the ground, adding to background levels. Another important man-made source is **medical use of radiation**, such as X-rays and other scans. Smaller contributions come from the **nuclear industry** and its waste.

bullets: **Location (rocks)**: areas with granite or other uranium-rich rocks have higher radon levels.
**Location (altitude)**: higher altitude gives more cosmic rays, so mountain areas have higher levels.
**Location (buildings)**: some buildings trap radon, especially if poorly ventilated.
**Occupation**: nuclear industry workers, radiographers and some medical staff receive extra dose.
**Occupation (air travel)**: aircraft crew and frequent flyers receive extra cosmic radiation at high altitude.
**Occupation (mining)**: miners and underground workers may be exposed to more radon.
Workers in radiation jobs wear **film badges** or dosimeters to monitor their dose.
Extra exposure is controlled using time, distance and shielding.
core.h: Variation of background radiation with location and occupation
core.p: Background radiation **is not the same everywhere**. The geology of an area matters because rocks such as granite release more radon. Altitude matters because there is less atmosphere to absorb cosmic rays. Occupation matters because some jobs bring extra exposure. This is why average values are quoted, and why examiners ask you to explain why two places or two people have different readings.

bullets: Background count rate = total counts / time.
**Corrected count rate = measured count rate − background count rate.**
Measuring for a **longer time** and repeating gives a more reliable average because decay is **random**.
Keep other sources **away** from the tube when measuring background.
Count rate is in counts per second or counts per minute.
The count rate decreases with **distance** from a source and with shielding.
A GM tube does not detect every decay, so the count rate is not the same as the true activity.
Background correction is especially important when measuring half-life of a weak source.
core.h: Measuring background radiation and correcting readings
core.p: A **Geiger-Muller (GM) tube** connected to a counter detects ionising radiation and records the **count rate**, the number of counts per second or minute. To find the background count rate you measure with **no source nearby** for a long time (for example several minutes) and divide the total counts by the time. When you later measure a source, the count includes the background too, so you must subtract it to obtain the **corrected count rate** that is due to the source alone.

bullets: **Unit of dose: sievert (Sv).**
**1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv)**, so 1 mSv = 0.001 Sv.
Dose measures **risk of harm**, whereas **activity** (in becquerel, Bq) measures how many decays occur per second.
A higher dose means a greater risk of damage such as cancer.
Very high doses delivered quickly cause radiation sickness.
Conversion example: 2.5 mSv = 0.0025 Sv; 0.4 Sv = 400 mSv.
Calculation of dose and risk is **not required**.
Dose limits are set for workers and the public, based on published evidence.
core.p: The **radiation dose** is a measure of the **risk of harm** to the body from exposure to radiation. It takes into account the type of radiation and the part of the body exposed, so it is not just the same as the activity of the source. Dose is measured in **sieverts (Sv)**. Because the sievert is a very large unit, doses are usually quoted in **millisieverts (mSv)**, where **1000 mSv = 1 Sv**. The specification states that you will not be required to calculate radiation dose or risk, but you must know the unit and the conversion.

bullets: Radiation **ionises** atoms in cells.
Damage to **DNA** can cause **mutations** and **cancer**.
Large doses **kill cells**, causing radiation sickness, burns and hair loss.
Effects of low doses may be **delayed** for many years.
**Gamma** is the main hazard outside the body; **alpha** is the main hazard inside the body.
Hazard is reduced using **time, distance and shielding** and by preventing contamination.
Some tissues, such as bone marrow and the foetus, are especially sensitive because their cells divide quickly.
Radiation hazards are balanced against benefits in medicine.
core.h: Hazards of radiation to the body
core.p: Ionising radiation harms living things because it ionises atoms in cells. If the DNA in a cell is altered the cell may **mutate** and divide in an uncontrolled way, causing **cancer**. If enough cells are killed, tissues and organs stop working properly, causing **radiation sickness**, and the skin can be burned. These effects may appear years after exposure, which makes low doses difficult to study. The harm depends on the **dose**, the **type of radiation** and whether the source is inside or outside the body.

bullets: **Medical tracers**: a radioactive isotope is injected or swallowed and collects in an organ; a **gamma camera** outside the body detects the gamma rays and builds an image of the organ.

Tracers must be **gamma emitters** so the radiation passes out of the body to be detected, and have a **short half-life** (a few hours, e.g. technetium-99m with a half-life of 6 hours) so that the patient is not exposed for long.
**Radiotherapy**: beams of gamma rays are directed at a tumour from several angles, so the dose to the tumour is high but the dose to healthy tissue is spread out.
Radiotherapy can also use a source placed **inside** the body near the tumour (for example iodine-131 for thyroid problems, which has a half-life of about 8 days).
**Sterilising** medical equipment: gamma rays kill microorganisms on sealed packages without heating, and without making the equipment radioactive.
Radiotherapy damages healthy cells as well as cancer cells, so side effects can occur.
Isotopes are chosen so that the radiation can be **detected** or **targeted** as needed.
The benefit (diagnosis or cure) is judged to outweigh the small risk.
core.h: Uses of nuclear radiation in medicine
core.p: Radiation has two main medical uses given in the specification: **exploration of internal organs** and the **control or destruction of unwanted tissue**. Doctors also use gamma rays to **sterilise** medical equipment. In each case the **type of radiation** and the **half-life** of the isotope are chosen to give the benefit with the smallest risk. Using a short half-life isotope means the patient is only radioactive for a short time.

bullets: **Smoke detectors**: contain an **alpha source** (americium-241, a long half-life) which ionises the air so a small current flows; smoke absorbs the alpha particles, the current drops and the alarm sounds. Alpha is used because it is strongly ionising and is stopped safely inside the detector.

**Thickness gauges**: a **beta source** is on one side of paper, plastic or aluminium foil and a detector on the other; thicker material absorbs more beta, so the count rate falls and the rollers are adjusted.
Alpha cannot be used for thickness gauges because it is stopped completely by the paper; gamma passes through almost unchanged so the count would not change with thickness.
**Food irradiation / sterilisation**: gamma rays kill bacteria so food lasts longer; the food does not become radioactive.
**Tracers in industry**: a gamma tracer in a pipe can detect leaks.
Sources used for long-term jobs need a **long half-life** so they do not need replacing often.
Sources used on the body need a **short half-life** so the exposure is brief.
The radiation must be able to do the job: it must either penetrate or ionise as required.
core.p: Beyond medicine, radioactive sources are used where their particular **penetrating power** and **half-life** suit the job. In each use, the type of radiation is chosen so that the property of the radiation is useful: alpha for ionising air, beta for materials that partly absorb it, and gamma for penetrating thick material or killing microbes.

bullets: Source **inside the body** as a tracer: gamma (leaves the body), short half-life.
Source **inside the body** for treatment of a small area: beta or alpha emitter, because it deposits its energy locally, with a suitable half-life.
Source **outside the body** for treatment: gamma, because it penetrates to the tumour.
**Sterilising** sealed items: gamma, because it penetrates the packaging.
**Smoke detector**: alpha, because of strong ionisation, with a long half-life so it lasts for years.
**Paper thickness**: beta, because some but not all passes through.
**Metal thickness (thick steel)**: gamma, because only gamma is penetrating enough.
Always state both the **radiation** and the **half-life** with reasons.
core.h: Choosing the right source: type of radiation and half-life
core.p: Many exam questions give a situation and ask which radioactive source is suitable. The method is simple: decide whether the radiation must **pass through** something (needs penetrating power, so gamma or beta) or **ionise** something (alpha), decide whether it is used **inside or outside** the body, and decide whether a **long or short half-life** is needed. Then write the reason for each choice.

bullets: **Risk**: ionisation can damage DNA and cause cancer; the risk rises with dose.
**Benefit**: diagnosing illness, treating cancer, sterilising equipment, fire safety, quality control in manufacturing.
**Precautions**: time, distance, shielding, sealed sources, monitoring, short half-life isotopes.
Medical doses are carefully controlled so that the benefit is much greater than the risk.
People may perceive radiation as high risk because the effects are **invisible, delayed and unfamiliar**.
Compare with everyday risks and with natural background radiation.
Reach a **judgement** and justify it with evidence, e.g. 'the benefit outweighs the small risk'.
Use balanced language and avoid emotional claims.
core.p: The specification requires you to **evaluate the perceived risks of nuclear radiation** in the light of the actual evidence. Perceived risk is how dangerous people **think** something is, which may differ from the real risk. Radiation is invisible, and the word 'nuclear' can sound frightening, so people may overestimate small risks such as those from medical scans, while underestimating others such as radon. A good evaluation compares the size of the **risk**, the **benefit** and the **precautions** taken, and uses reliable evidence.

bullets: **Peer review** = checking by independent experts before publication.
Publication allows other scientists to **repeat and check** the results.
It helps to **reduce bias** and improve accuracy.
Long-term effects such as cancer need studies of **large groups over many years**.
Evidence from the studies is used to set **safe working limits**.
The public is better informed, helping to reduce wrong perceptions of risk.
Be ready to explain why a result that has not been peer reviewed should be treated with caution.
This idea appears across the science specification, not just in physics.
core.p: Studies into the effects of radiation on humans are **published** so that other scientists can see the methods and results. Before publication they are **peer reviewed**: independent experts check the work to see that the methods and conclusions are sound. This makes the evidence more **reliable**, lets others **repeat** the study, and helps governments decide safe dose limits. Without sharing results, mistakes or bias could go unnoticed, and the public could not trust the safety rules.

bullets: Half-life link: a tracer with a 6 hour half-life falls to 1/16 of its activity after 24 hours.
Count rate link: the corrected count rate equals the measured count rate minus background.
Contamination link: tracers inside the body make the patient contaminated for a short time.
Alpha link: radon is an alpha emitter, dangerous if inhaled.
Nuclear power link: waste contains long half-life isotopes and adds to man-made background.
Electromagnetic spectrum link: gamma is the most energetic electromagnetic radiation.
Units link: dose in Sv or mSv; activity in Bq; count rate in counts per second or minute.
Evaluate: always weigh benefit against risk and mention precautions.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier thinking
core.p: This point connects to **types of radiation** (penetration and ionisation decide the use), **half-life** (decides how long a source remains active), **irradiation and contamination** (decides the hazard to a patient or worker) and **nuclear equations** (the isotope emitting the radiation). Higher-tier questions often combine them: you may be given a decay graph, asked for the half-life, and then asked whether the isotope is suitable as a medical tracer. Use numbers from the graph and state the reason.

exam: **Name two sources (2 marks):** one natural (radon, cosmic rays, rocks, food) and one man-made (nuclear weapons fallout, nuclear accidents, medical).
**Why does background vary? (2-3 marks):** link to location (granite rocks, radon, altitude) or occupation (nuclear workers, aircrew, radiographers).
**Corrected count rate:** subtract the background count rate; convert to the same time unit first.
**Unit conversions:** 1000 mSv = 1 Sv; multiply by 1000 to go to mSv and divide by 1000 to go to Sv.
**'Why is a tracer suitable?':** gamma emitter so it passes out of the body, short half-life so it does not stay radioactive for long.
**'Why is beta used in a thickness gauge?':** alpha is stopped by the paper, gamma passes straight through, beta is partly absorbed so the count rate changes with thickness.
**Smoke detector:** alpha ionises the air; smoke absorbs alpha and reduces the current; alarm sounds.
**Evaluate (4-6 marks):** state a benefit, state a risk, mention precautions, then give a justified judgement.
**Peer review:** say that independent experts check the method and conclusions so the evidence is reliable.
**Command words:** 'Suggest' needs applying ideas to unfamiliar situations; 'Evaluate' needs a judgement with evidence for and against.
**Data questions:** subtract background first, then read half-life from the corrected values.

mistakes.r: It is mostly natural (radon, cosmic rays, rocks, food); man-made sources such as weapons fallout, accidents and medical add a smaller amount.
It is always present, from the environment, and must be subtracted from readings.
mistakes.w: Background radiation is caused by the source being tested.

mistakes.r: Corrected count rate = measured count rate minus background count rate.
Medical tracers have a short half-life so the patient is not exposed for long.
mistakes.w: Tracers should have a long half-life so they last longer.

mistakes.r: Tracers are gamma emitters so the radiation passes out of the body and can be detected.
Alpha would be stopped by the paper; beta is used because some passes through and the amount depends on thickness.
mistakes.w: Alpha is used for thickness gauges.

mistakes.r: Gamma irradiation of food kills bacteria but does not make the food radioactive.
Radiation also damages healthy cells, so beams are aimed from several directions to reduce this.

summary: The specification asks you to know the natural and man-made sources of background radiation, why it varies with location and occupation, the unit of dose (sieverts), the hazards of radiation, and the uses of radioactive sources in medicine and industry. You must evaluate risks against benefits and match type of radiation and half-life to each use. It matters because it explains how radiation is used safely every day.

terms.d: Low-level ionising radiation that is around us all the time, from natural and man-made sources.
A radioactive gas, an alpha emitter, produced by decay of uranium in rocks; the largest single natural source of background radiation.
High-energy particles from space and the Sun that add to background radiation, more at high altitude.
A measure of the risk of harm from exposure to radiation, in sieverts (Sv).
The unit of radiation dose; 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 Sv.
The number of counts per unit time detected by a Geiger-Muller tube.
The measured count rate minus the background count rate.
A detector that produces a pulse each time ionising radiation enters it, used with a counter to measure count rate.
A radioactive isotope used in medicine to explore internal organs; it is detected outside the body.
Use of ionising radiation to control or destroy unwanted tissue such as cancer cells.
The time taken for the number of radioactive nuclei to halve, or for the count rate or activity to fall to half its initial value.
Killing microorganisms on equipment or food, e.g. with gamma rays.
The removal of electrons from atoms to form ions; ionising radiation damages living cells in this way.
Checking of research by independent experts before it is published.
How risky people think something is, which may differ from the actual risk.

worked.q: A student measures 60 counts in 5 minutes with no source present. With a source nearby she measures 396 counts in 3 minutes. Calculate the corrected count rate. (3 marks)
steps: Background count rate = 60 / 5 = 12 counts per minute.
Measured count rate = 396 / 3 = 132 counts per minute.
Corrected count rate = 132 − 12 = 120 counts per minute.

worked.ans: Gamma leaves the body to be detected and is weakly ionising, and its short half-life limits the time the patient is exposed.
worked.q: Technetium-99m is a gamma emitter with a half-life of 6 hours and is used as a medical tracer. Explain why it is suitable. (4 marks)
steps: Gamma rays can pass out of the body so they can be detected by a gamma camera outside (1).
Gamma is weakly ionising so there is less damage to cells inside the body (1).
A short half-life of 6 hours means that the tracer decays quickly (1).
So the patient is exposed to radiation for only a short time, reducing the risk (1).

worked.ans: Alpha ionises the air giving a current; smoke reduces this current and triggers the alarm.
worked.q: Explain how a smoke detector containing americium-241 works and why an alpha source is used. (4 marks)
steps: The alpha particles ionise the air between two electrodes (1).
This allows a small current to flow (1).
Smoke absorbs the alpha particles so the current falls and the alarm sounds (1).
Alpha is used because it is strongly ionising and is stopped by the detector casing, and a long half-life means it works for years (1).
